title: Organic User Acquisition for Apps: Connecting TikTok and AI Search
summary: An, founder of Flamme, joins Tenjin's ROI 101 to explain how TikTok, AI search, and organic creative testing can support app acquisition.
body_markdown:
It happens all the time: someone watches a TikTok about your app, likes it, then scrolls on. Two days later, they ask ChatGPT for an app that solves a problem your app also solves. But, if your app isn’t mentioned or recommended at all, all that attention and demand might go to a competitor app.


An Nayal, founder of the couples app Flamme, calls that a leak and he built his growth strategy around closing that gap. On Tenjin’s ROI 101 podcast, he explains how he scaled Flamme with organic social and GEO. He also reveals where and how he would use a $10,000 monthly budget if he had to start all over again.


## Flamme’s Organic Growth Experience


Organic user acquisition for apps is when you can users without having to pay for ad placements on various channels from social, to app store searches, web search, and AI recommendations. Flamme is just one example of a couples app that grew this way. An shares:


> *We scaled it purely using organic, using TikTok organic, using Instagram organic, using GEO.*


This lesson isn’t going to be about just one channel. It focuses more on the ecosystem of channels that support, connect, and help each other. For Flamme, social content was used as discovery, putting it front and center for new audiences. GEO helped the app show up and that it was described accurately when people looked for it.


## Where to Put a $10,000 Monthly Budget?


An would start with social content and give it an initial three-month period to work.


> *If someone is just starting with 10K a month, what I recommend initially is socials. So the initial goal, 10K a month, put it into TikTok for three months.*


This three month period gives enough time for a team to test formats, learn what resonates, build consistency, and learn the best posting schedule. Let’s remember that just because it is organic, it doesn’t translate into no cost or it being free. Much of the budget has to go towards producers and creators, editing, tools, and also your team’s time.


Before setting out to test An’s recommendation check whether it fits your app.


**Question** **If Yes** **If No**


Does your audience spend time on TikTok or Instagram? Social is a good place to start Start where your audience already is, such as communities, search, or partnerships


Can your team publish useful content every week? Plan a three-month test Solve capacity first, or work with creators


Is your app easy to show in a short video? Lead with demos Lead with the problem and the outcome


Do people already search for apps in your category? Make sure your website and listings are ready to catch that demand Social may need to create the demand first


Remember, this is An’s recommendation for a hypothetical app budget, not a tested formula for every app. The budget comes as part of a package that includes an accurate store listing and optimized website.


After three months, evaluate your results based on the engagement and what happened after that. It’s more than just views.


**After Three Months** **Suggestion** **Next Steps**


Strong views, few profile visits or installs The hook works, but people don’t connect it to the app Make the problem-to-app link clearer in captions and your profile


Repeated comments asking what the app does or costs Interest, but information is missing Answer it on your website and store listing, then check AI answers


Organic installs and store searches for your app’s name rise with posting Social is creating demand Keep posting, and test the best ideas on paid


Little movement on any signal Wrong platform, format or audience Change one thing, or move budget to where your audience is


## Social Discovery Leads to Search


For An, social content and AI search have two different, but related buckets. Social is able to create the demand and then GEO should be the one that captures their attention at any later point in time.


> *As TikTok creates demand, GEO catches the people who then ask an AI.*


These two channels are very popular for app discovery and continue to grow. In an **[AppTweak survey](https://www.apptweak.com/en/aso-blog/ai-app-discovery-survey)** of 1,000 US adults, 10.4% said they first heard about their most recent app or game download on social media, and 10.0% from an AI assistant, next to Google Search at 10.7%.


And although he likes to use the two related buckets analogy, he still frames it as a bit of a “chicken and the egg” scenario, mostly because even though social might get you that first inch of traction, the audience and potential users might not respond right away.


> *What eventually happens is that when people see the traction there, they’ll go and search for you and they’ll try to locate you on these engines.*


Based from what An shared, we can call this the Social to Search Model. It has four steps:


1. **Discover:** someone sees a video about a problem, or about your app.
2. **Research:** later, they ask an AI assistant for options, suitability, or pricing.
3. **Compare:** they weigh the shortlist the answer gives them.
4. **Decide:** they install, or they don’t.


For example, there’s a language learning app that posts a video about practicing conversation for 10 minutes a day. A viewer likes it but doesn’t install. A few days later, the same viewers ask ChatGPT for the best app to practice German conversation as a beginner. If the answer from the AI engine doesn’t mention the app, or if they get the price wrong, then it’s almost like that language app never existed and instead, it will go to a different language app that offers German.


> *Capture that leak by coming into the GEO side.*


Consistency is how you capture GEO. It’s important to use the same app name, the same use cases, and the same claims in your social profiles and captions, on your website, and in your store listings. It’s all part of your brand identity.


## Make Your Website Useful When People Look You Up


When someone sees your app in a video and wants to know more, your website is often where they go to learn more about your app and brand. Every app needs its own website.


> *Everyone expects businesses to have a website, and an app is a business, end of day.*


Someone researching your app after seeing a video usually wants answers to four questions:


- Is this app for me?
- What does it actually do?
- What does it cost?
- Which devices does it support?


If you are able to answer these questions clearly, then you can aid two kinds of visitors simultaneously: humans and AI bots, the AI systems that need a reliable source to describe your app. For a full checklist of what you should include, see the website section of our ****[guide to GEO for mobile apps](https://tenjin.com/blog/blog-geo-for-mobile-apps/) **.**


The connection between social media and AI search can work the other way around too. With one client of Agniverse, the media house and GEO search lab he runs, An noticed that:


> *…the social content actually created a GEO presence for them, because social content is also heavily, heavily read by AI engines.*


But this is just one example and not a definitive rule. A viral video still won’t be able to guarantee a citation, a recommendation, or an install, but it’s another reason to keep what you say about your app consistent everywhere.


## Use Organic Response to Shape Your Paid Creative Tests


An’s advice to founders is to “look at socials like it’s an untapped gold mine.” Testing organic posts lets you find out which ideas people actually respond to before you spend money to scale them.


> *Paid ads is a good classic approach, and it really works, but social can complement that by helping you understand what can really scale organically. Test that organically before you start putting it out on paid.*


And, here’s a simple way to put this idea into practice:


- Post several audience problems and hooks as organic content.
- Look at how people respond: views, comments, saves, shares, and profile visits.
- Pick the ideas that get the strongest response from the right people.
- Run a controlled paid test with those ideas.
- Check what happens after the install, like retention, trial starts, and revenue.


Each organic signal tells you something different:


**Signal** **Answer**


Views and watch time Whether this problem matters to your audience or not


Questions in comments What information people are missing


Profile and link clicks Whether people want to learn more


Installs and in-app behavior Whether these are the uses you want or not


You should not expect organic wins to carry over to paid automatically. Paid campaigns reach different people through different systems so let the organic results narrow your shortlist, then judge the paid test on its own numbers.


When you are ready to move to paid social and ad networks, then[Tenjin’s ROI dashboard](https://tenjin.com/roi-dashboard/) shows campaign cost, revenue, and ROI side by side, so you can see which concepts bring valuable users. Keep in mind that a person who sees an organic video and installs days later usually can’t be tied back to that specific video. But that’s normal and it’s why the controlled paid test matters.


## Measure the Installs That Organic Content Drives


Installs that begin with an organic video usually show up as organic in your reports, because people often research the app later in an AI assistant or the app store before they install. You can’t attribute each one, but you can see the pattern:


- **Ask new users:** add both “TikTok or Instagram” and “An AI assistant” as options in a “How did you hear about us?” onboarding question.
- **Tag your profile link:** if your bio links to your website, carry the tracking parameters through to the download button. Otherwise those installs also count as organic.
- **Watch store search installs:** App Store Connect and Google Play Console both report installs from store search, and Play Console shows the search terms. A rise in searches for your app’s name after a strong post is a signal, not proof.
- **Check AI answers after a post performs well:** see whether assistants mention your app for the problem the video showed. Our guide to measuring your app’s visibility in AI search explains how.
- **Judge users on value, not volume:** people who research before installing often pay later, so compare day 7 and day 30 revenue by source, not just installs.


## Build a Repeatable Acquisition Process


You don’t need a complicated system to make organic work. It comes down to three main things:


1. Pick one user problem your app can show clearly.
2. Make your app easy to find and research: a clear website, accurate listings, and consistent claims.
3. Decide how you’ll judge the next test before you run it.


Organic content takes resources even without media spend. It needs to be treated like any other channel, with a budget, an owner, and success criteria.


To measure how visibility in AI answers changes over time, see our guide on **measuring your app’s visibility in AI search** . For acquisition beyond organic, read our **[user acquisition strategy guide](https://tenjin.com/blog/blog-app-user-acquisition-strategy/) ,** which looks at user value past day-7 ROAS.


## Key Takeaways


- Social creates demand, GEO catches it. People who discover your app on social often look it up later in an AI assistant, so make sure they find you there.
- Start with social. With $10,000 a month, An recommends putting it into social content for an initial three months.
- Test organically, then validate with paid. Organic results help you choose which ideas to test, but they don’t replace a proper paid test.
- Stay consistent. Use the same app name, use cases, and pricing across social, your website, and your store listings.
- Measure what attribution misses. Installs that start with an organic video often show up as organic, so ask new users how they found you and watch installs from store search.


## Frequently Asked Questions


****What is organic user acquisition for apps?****


Organic user acquisition for apps is gaining users without paying for ad placements, through channels like social content, app store search, web search, AI assistant recommendations, and word of mouth. It still takes time and creative work, and sometimes creator fees.


****Can TikTok drive app installs without paid ads?****


For some apps, yes. An Nayal, founder of Flamme, scaled his app with organic TikTok and Instagram alongside GEO. Whether it works for you depends on whether your audience is on the platform, whether your app is easy to show in a short video, and whether you can post consistently.


****How do social content and AI search work together?****


Social content gets people interested in a problem or an app, and they often look it up later. In An’s model, TikTok creates the demand, and GEO makes sure your app shows up, described accurately, when those people ask an AI assistant for options.


****Does strong organic engagement predict paid ad performance?****


Not reliably. It’s a great way to choose which ideas to test, but paid campaigns reach different people through different systems. Run a controlled paid test on your best ideas, and measure what users do after they install.


****What should app teams measure beyond views?****


Look at questions in comments, profile and link clicks, installs, and what users do after installing, like retention, trial starts, and revenue. Views tell you what’s relevant, while post-install behavior tells you whether those users are worth having.


****How can I tell if TikTok content is driving installs I can’t attribute?****


Installs that start with an organic TikTok video usually show up as organic, because people often research the app later in an AI assistant or the app store. Ask new users how they found you, compare your posting calendar with installs from store search, and test your strongest ideas on paid campaigns, where attribution is possible.
